newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Aid donors have potential to pressure Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Aid donors have potential to pressure Cambodia.

text.p: Cambodia's major aid donors are expected to seek ways to co-ordinate policies for greater leverage on Phnom Penh to end the crisis in the turbulent Asian kingdom, diplomatic sources said on Saturday.
The sources said, however, the nine-member Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) had the lead role to play in fostering peace and stability in Cambodia.

Cambodia took centre stage during the two-day annual meeting of ASEAN foreign ministers that ended on Friday, and is a major topic as other Asian and Western powers gather for a regional security session on Sunday and bilateral meetings.

The crisis erupted in early July when Second Prime Minister Hun Sen ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, son of King Sihanouk, in a putsch in which at least 35 people are believed to have died.

Cambodia was due to have joined ASEAN, together with Burma and Laos, this week, but its admittance was postponed due to the turmoil. The grouping now comprises Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore, Vietnam, the Philippines, Brunei, Burma and Laos.
Three ASEAN foreign minister headed by Indonesia's Ali Alatas conducted an abortive mediation bid after the decision to postpone Cambodia's membership in ASEAN.
Diplomats have said Alatas came away from Phnom Penh last weekend furious after being "subjected to a two-hour lecture by Hun Sen".

The diplomatic sources said Australia saw aid as one way of putting pressure on Hun Sen to meet political and human rights conditions to end the crisis. Canberra had made its aid, running at A$32 million (US$24 million) this year, conditional on a return to normality.
France, the United States and Australia are major donors, although their contributions are dwarfed by Japan's aid to the kingdom, which diplomats described as the most aid-dependent country on earth.
Washington has frozen its aid to Cambodia for a month, and the sources said it was critical to reach an agreement on co-ordination between all four donors to make leverage effective.
Diplomatic sources said it was essential to bring both the United States and Japan into a coordinated aid policy.

They said it would be helpful if the United States, represented by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright at the Kuala Lumpur meetings, "came out and said ASEAN had a leading role" in finding a solution in Cambodia.
Albright told reporters on her way to Malaysia that Hun Sen's apparent agreement on ASEAN mediation was important, but noted an ambiguous aspect to his comments.
"I'm not convinced of anything until I see it," she said.
ASEAN ministers have asked Cambodia's Foreign Minister Ung Huot to find out exactly what is Hun Sen's attitude towards ASEAN mediation after confusing reports from Phnom Penh.
Hun Sen said on Friday ASEAN's role should be to prevent "foreign interference in the internal affairs of Cambodia" and that the country's problems should be resolved internally.
Diplomats have said ASEAN was showing "really remarkable strength and maturity" in dealing with the Cambodian situation.

Cambodia has been on top of the ASEAN agenda through two decades of turmoil. Member states, particularly Indonesia, were influential in bringing about the 1991 Paris peace accords, which were followed by U.N.-organised elections in 1993 that brought Prince Ranariddh and Hun Sen to power in a coalition government.
